Some Properties of and Open Problems on Hessian Nilpotent PolynomialsThanks: The author has been partially supported by NSA Grant R1-07-0053

Wenhua Zhao
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

In the recent work [BE1], [M], [Z1] and [Z2], the well-known Jacobian conjecture ([BCW], [E]) has been reduced to a problem on HN (Hessian nilpotent) polynomials (the polynomials whose Hessian matrix are nilpotent) and their (deformed) inversion pairs. In this paper, we prove several results on HN polynomials, their (deformed) inversion pairs as well as on the associated symmetric polynomial or formal maps. We also propose some open problems for further study of these objects.

Key words and phrases: 
Hessian nilpotent polynomials, inversion pairs, harmonic polynomials, the Jacobian conjecture.
2000 Mathematics Subject Classification
14R15, 32H02, 32A50

1. Introduction

In the recent work [BE1], [M], [Z1] and [Z2], the well-known Jacobian conjecture (see [BCW] and [E]) has been reduced to a problem on HN (Hessian nilpotent) polynomials, i.e. the polynomials whose Hessian matrix are nilpotent, and their (deformed) inversion pairs. In this paper, we prove some properties of HN polynomials, the (deformed) inversion pairs of (HN) polynomial, the associated symmetric polynomial or formal maps, the graphs assigned to homogeneous harmonic polynomials, etc. Another purpose of this paper is to draw the reader’s attention to some open problems which we believe will be interesting and important for further study of these objects.

In this section we first discuss some backgrounds and motivations in Subsection 1.1 for the study of HN polynomials and their (deformed) inversion pairs. We also fix some terminology and notation in this subsection that will be used throughout this paper. Then in Subsection 1.2 we give an arrangement description of this paper.

1.1. Background and Motivation

Let z=(z1,z2,…,zn)z=(z_{1},z_{2},\dots,z_{n}) be nn free commutative variables. We denote by ℂ⁡[z]\mathbb{C}[z] (resp. ℂ⁡[[z]]\mathbb{C}[[z]]) the algebra of polynomials (resp. formal power series) of zz over ℂ\mathbb{C}. A polynomial or formal power series P⁡(z)P(z) is said to be HN (Hessian nilpotent) if its Hessian matrix Hes ​P:=(∂2P∂zi​∂zj)\text{Hes\,}P\!:=(\frac{\partial^{2}P}{\partial z_{i}\partial z_{j}}) are nilpotent. The study of HN polynomials is mainly motivated by the recent progress achieved in [BE1], [M], [Z1] and [Z2] on the well-known JC (Jacobian conjecture), which we will briefly explain below.

Recall that the JC first proposed by Keller [Ke] in 1939 claims: for any polynomial map FF of ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} with the Jacobian j⁡(F)=1j(F)=1, its formal inverse map GG must also be a polynomial map. Despite intense study for more than half a century, the conjecture is still open even for the case n=2n=2. For more history and known results before 20002000 on the Jacobian conjecture, see [BCW], [E] and references there. In 20032003, M. de Bondt, A. van den Essen ([BE1]) and G. Meng ([M]) independently made the following breakthrough on the JC.

Let Di:=∂∂ziD_{i}\!:=\frac{\partial}{\partial z_{i}} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n) and D=(D1,…,Dn)D=(D_{1},\dots,D_{n}). For any P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[z]], denote by ∇P​(z)\nabla P(z) the gradient of P⁡(z)P(z), i.e. ∇P​(z):=(D1​P​(z),…,Dn​P​(z))\nabla P(z):=(D_{1}P(z),\dots,D_{n}P(z)). We say a formal map F⁡(z)=z−H⁡(z)F(z)=z-H(z) is symmetric if H​(z)=∇P​(z)H(z)=\nabla P(z) for some P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[z]]. Then, the symmetric reduction of the JC achieved in [BE1] and [M] is that, to prove or disprove the JC, it will be enough to consider only symmetric polynomial maps. Combining with the classical homogeneous reduction achieved in [BCW] and [Y], one may further assume that the symmetric polynomial maps have the form F​(z)=z−∇P​(z)F(z)=z-\nabla P(z) with P⁡(z)P(z) homogeneous ((of degree 44)). Note that, in this case the Jacobian condition j⁡(F)=1j(F)=1 is equivalent to the condition that P⁡(z)P(z) is HN. For some other recent results on symmetric polynomial or formal maps, see [BE1]–[BE5], [EW], [M], [Wr1], [Wr2], [Z1], [Z2] and [EZ].

Based on the homogeneous reduction and the symmetric reduction of the JC discussed above, the author further showed in [Z2] that the JC is actually equivalent to the following so-called vanishing conjecture of HN polynomials.

Conjecture 1.1.

((Vanishing Conjecture)) Let Δ:=∑i=1nDi2\Delta\!:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}D_{i}^{2} be the Laplace operator of ℂ⁡[z]\mathbb{C}[z]. Then, for any HN polynomial P⁡(z)P(z) ((of homogeneous of degree d=4d=4)), Δm​Pm+1​(z)=0\Delta^{m}P^{m+1}(z)=0 when m>>0m>>0.

Furthermore, the following criterion of Hessian nilpotency for formal power series was also proved in [Z2].

Proposition 1.2.

For any P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[z]] with o⁡(P⁡(z))≥2o(P(z))\geq 2, the following statements are equivalent.

  1. (1)

    P⁡(z)P(z) is HN.

  2. (2)

    Δm​Pm=0\Delta^{m}P^{m}=0 for any m≥1m\geq 1.

  3. (3)

    Δm​Pm=0\Delta^{m}P^{m}=0 for any 1≤m≤n1\leq m\leq n.

One crucial idea of the proofs in [Z2] for the results above is to study a special formal deformation of symmetric formal maps. More precisely, let tt be a central formal parameter. For any P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[z]], we call F​(z)=z−∇P​(z)F(z)=z-\nabla P(z) the associated symmetric maps of P⁡(z)P(z). Let Ft(z)=z−t∇P(z)F_{t}(z)\>=z-t\nabla P(z). When the order o⁡(P⁡(z))o(P(z)) of P⁡(z)P(z) with respect to zz is greater than or equal to 22, Ft​(z)F_{t}(z) is a formal map of ℂ​[[t]]​[[z]]\mathbb{C}[[t]][[z]] with Ft=1​(z)=F​(z)F_{t=1}(z)=F(z). Therefore, we may view Ft​(z)F_{t}(z) as a formal deformation of the formal map F⁡(z)F(z). In this case, one can also show (see [M] or Lemma 3.143.14 in [Z1]) that the formal inverse map Gt​(z):=Ft−1​(z)G_{t}(z)\!:=F_{t}^{-1}(z) of Ft​(z)F_{t}(z) does exist and is also symmetric, i.e. there exists a unique Qt​(z)∈ℂ⁡[[t]]​[[z]]Q_{t}(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[t]][[z]] with o⁡(Qt​(z))≥2o(Q_{t}(z))\geq 2 such that Gt(z)=z+t∇Qt(z)G_{t}(z)=z+t\nabla Q_{t}(z). We call Qt​(z)Q_{t}(z) the deformed inversion pair of P⁡(z)P(z). Note that, whenever Qt=1​(z)Q_{t=1}(z) makes sense, the formal inverse map G⁡(z)G(z) of F⁡(z)F(z) is given by G⁡(z)=Gt=1​(z)=z+∇Qt=1​(z)G(z)=G_{t=1}(z)=z+\nabla Q_{t=1}(z), so in this case we call Q​(z):=Qt=1​(z)Q(z)\!:=Q_{t=1}(z) the inversion pair of P⁡(z)P(z).

Note that, under the condition o⁡(P⁡(z))≥2o(P(z))\geq 2, the deformed inversion pair Qt​(z)Q_{t}(z) of P⁡(z)P(z) might not be in ℂ​[t]​[[z]]\mathbb{C}[t][[z]], so Qt=1​(z)Q_{t=1}(z) may not make sense. But, if we assume further that J​(Ft)​(0)=1J(F_{t})(0)=1, or equivalently, (Hes ​P)​(0)(\text{Hes\,}P)(0) is nilpotent, then Ft​(z)F_{t}(z) is an automorphism of ℂ​[t]​[[z]]\mathbb{C}[t][[z]], hence so is its inverse map Gt​(z)G_{t}(z). Therefore, in this case Qt​(z)Q_{t}(z) lies in ℂ​[t]​[[z]]\mathbb{C}[t][[z]] and Qt=1​(z)Q_{t=1}(z) makes sense. Throughout this paper, whenever the inversion pair Q⁡(z)Q(z) of a polynomial or formal power series P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[z]] (not necessarily HN) is under concern, our assumption on P⁡(z)P(z) will always be o⁡(P⁡(z))≥2o(P(z))\geq 2 and (Hes ​P)​(0)(\text{Hes\,}P)(0) is nilpotent. Note that, for any HN P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[z]] with o⁡(P⁡(z))≥2o(P(z))\geq 2, the condition that (Hes ​P)​(0)(\text{Hes\,}P)(0) is nilpotent holds automatically.

For later purpose, let us recall the following formula derived in [Z2] for the deformed inversion pairs of HN formal power series.

Theorem 1.3.

Suppose P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[z]] with o⁡(P⁡(z))≥2o(P(z))\geq 2 is HN. Then, we have

(1.1) Qt​(z)\displaystyle Q_{t}(z) =∑m=0∞tm2m​m!​(m+1)!​Δm​Pm+1​(z),\displaystyle=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{t^{m}}{2^{m}m!(m+1)!}\Delta^{m}P^{m+1}(z),

From the equivalence of the JC and the VC discussed above, we see that the study on the HN polynomials and their (deformed) inversion pairs becomes important and necessary, at least when the JC is concerned. Note that, due to the identity Tr Hes ​P=Δ​P\mbox{Tr\,}\text{Hes\,}P=\Delta P, HN polynomials are just a special family of harmonic polynomials which are among the most classical objects in mathematics. Even though harmonic polynomials had been very well studied since the late of the eighteenth century, it seems that not much has been known on HN polynomials. We believe that these mysterious (HN) polynomials deserve much more attentions from mathematicians.

1.2. Arrangement

Considering the length of this paper, we here give a more detailed arrangement description of the paper.

In Section 2, we consider the following two questions. Let P,S,T∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P,S,T\in\mathbb{C}[[z]] with P=S+TP=S+T and Q,U,VQ,U,V their inversion pairs, respectively.

𝐐𝟏{\bf Q_{1}}: Under what conditions, PP is HN iff both SS and TT are HN?

𝐐𝟐{\bf Q_{2}}: Under what conditions, we have Q=U+VQ=U+V?

We give some sufficient conditions in Theorems 2.1 and 2.7 for the two questions above. In Section 3, we employ a recursion formula of inversion pairs derived in [Z1] and Eq. (1.1)(\ref{E-Q-1}) above to derive some estimates for the radius of convergence of inversion pairs of homogeneous (HN) polynomials (see Propositions 3.1 and 3.3).

For any P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[z]], we say it is self-inverting if its inversion pair Q⁡(z)Q(z) is P⁡(z)P(z) itself. In Section 4, by using a general result on quasi-translations proved in [B], we derive some properties of HN self-inverting formal power series P⁡(z)P(z). Another purpose of this section is to draw the reader’s attention to Open Problem 4.8 on classification of HN self-inverting polynomials or formal power series.

In Section 5, we show in Proposition 5.1, when the base field has characteristic p>0p>0, the VC, unlike the JC, actually holds for any polynomials P⁡(z)P(z) even without the HN condition on P⁡(z)P(z). It also holds in this case for any HN formal power series. One interesting question (see Open Problem 5.2) is to see if the VC like the JC fails over ℂ\mathbb{C} when P⁡(z)P(z) is allowed to be any HN formal power series.

In Section 6, we prove a criterion of Hessian nilpotency for homogeneous polynomials over ℂ\mathbb{C} (see Theorem 6.1). Considering the criterion in Proposition 1.2, this criterion is somewhat surprising but its proof turns out to be very simple.

Section 7 is mainly motivated by the following question raised by M. Kumar ([K]) and D. Wright ([Wr3]). Namely, for a symmetric formal map F​(z)=z−∇P​(z)F(z)=z-\nabla P(z), how to write f⁡(z):=12​σ2−P⁡(z)f(z)\!:=\frac{1}{2}\sigma_{2}-P(z) (where σ2:=∑i=1nzi2\sigma_{2}\!:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}^{2}) and P⁡(z)P(z) itself as formal power series in F⁡(z)F(z)? In this section, we derive some explicit formulas to answer the questions above and also for the same question for σ2\sigma_{2} (see Proposition 7.2). From these formulas, we also show in Theorem 7.4 that, the VC holds for a HN polynomial P⁡(z)P(z) iff one (hence, all) of σ2\sigma_{2}, P⁡(z)P(z) and f⁡(z)f(z) can be written as a polynomial in FF, where F​(z)=z−∇P​(z)F(z)=z-\nabla P(z) is the associated polynomial maps of P⁡(z)P(z).

Finally, in Section 8, we discuss a graph 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P) assigned to each homogeneous harmonic polynomials P⁡(z)P(z). The graph 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P) was first proposed by the author and later was further studied by Roel Willems in his master thesis [Wi] under direction of Professor Arno van den Essen. In Subsection 8.1 we give the definition of the graph 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P) for any homogeneous harmonic polynomial P⁡(z)P(z) and discuss the connectedness reduction (see Corollary 8.5) which says, to study the VC for homogeneous HN polynomials P⁡(z)P(z), it will be enough to consider the case when the graph 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P) is connected. In Subsection 8.2 we consider a connection of 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P) with the tree expansion formula derived in [M] and [Wr2] for the inversion pair Q⁡(z)Q(z) of P⁡(z)P(z) (see also Proposition 8.9). As an application of the connection, we use it to give another proof for the connectedness reduction discussed in Corollary 8.5.

One final remark on the paper is as follows. Even though we could have focused only on (HN) polynomials, at least when only the JC is concerned, we will formulate and prove our results in the more general setting of (HN) formal power series whenever it is possible.

Acknowledgement: The author is very grateful to Professors Arno van den Essen, Mohan Kumar and David Wright for inspiring communications and constant encouragement. Section 7 was mainly motivated by some questions raised by Professors Mohan Kumar and David Wright. The author also would like to thank Roel Willems for sending the author his master thesis in which he has obtained some very interesting results on the graphs 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P) of homogeneous harmonic polynomials. At last but not the least, the author thanks the referee and the editor for many valuable suggestions.

2. Disjoint Formal Power Series and Their Deformed Inversion Pairs

Let P,S,T∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P,S,T\in\mathbb{C}[[z]] with P=S+TP=S+T, and QQ, UU and VV their inversion pairs, respectively. In this section, we consider the following two questions:

  1. 𝐐𝟏{\bf{Q_{1}}}:

    Under what conditions, PP is HN if and only if both SS and TT are HN?

  2. 𝐐𝟐{\bf Q_{2}}:

    Under what conditions, we have Q=U+VQ=U+V?

We give some answers to the questions 𝐐𝟏{\bf Q_{1}} and 𝐐𝟐{\bf Q_{2}} in Theorems 2.1 and 2.7, respectively. The results proved here will also be needed in Section 8 when we consider a graph associated to homogeneous harmonic polynomials.

To question 𝐐𝟏{\bf Q_{1}} above, we have the following result.

Theorem 2.1.

Let S,T∈ℂ⁡[[z]]S,T\in\mathbb{C}[[z]] such that ⟨∇(Di​S),∇(Dj​T)⟩=0\langle\nabla(D_{i}S),\nabla(D_{j}T)\rangle=0 for any 1≤i,j≤n1\leq i,j\leq n, where ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle denotes the standard ℂ\mathbb{C}-bilinear form of ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}. Let P=S+TP=S+T. Then, we have

  1. (a)(a)

    Hes ​(S)​Hes ​(T)=Hes ​(T)​Hes ​(S)=0.\text{Hes\,}(S)\,\text{Hes\,}(T)=\text{Hes\,}(T)\,\text{Hes\,}(S)=0.

  2. (b)(b)

    PP is HN iff both SS and TT are HN.

Note that statement (b)(b) in the theorem above was first proved by R. Willems ([Wi]) in a special setting as in Lemma 2.6 below for homogeneous harmonic polynomials.

Proof:  (a)(a) For any 1≤i,j≤n1\leq i,j\leq n, consider the (i,j)t​h(i,j)^{th} entry of the product Hes ​(S)​Hes ​(T)\text{Hes\,}(S)\text{Hes\,}(T):

(2.1) ∑k=1n∂2S∂zi​∂zk​∂2T∂zk​∂zj=⟨∇(Di​S),∇(Dj​T)⟩=0.\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{\partial^{2}S}{\partial z_{i}\partial z_{k}}\frac{\partial^{2}T}{\partial z_{k}\partial z_{j}}=\langle\nabla(D_{i}S),\nabla(D_{j}T)\rangle=0.

Hence Hes ​(S)​Hes ​(T)=0\text{Hes\,}(S)\,\text{Hes\,}(T)=0. Similarly, we have Hes ​(T)​Hes ​(S)=0\text{Hes\,}(T)\,\text{Hes\,}(S)=0.

(b)(b) follows directly from (a)(a) and the lemma below.  □\Box

Lemma 2.2.

Let AA, BB and CC be n×nn\times n matrices with entries in any commutative ring. Suppose that A=B+CA=B+C and B​C=C​B=0BC=CB=0. Then, AA is nilpotent iff both BB and CC are nilpotent.

Proof:  The (⇐)(\Leftarrow) part is trivial because BB and CC in particular commute with each other.

To show (⇒)(\Rightarrow), note that B​C=C​B=0BC=CB=0. So for any m≥1m\geq 1, we have

Am​B=(B+C)m​B=(Bm+Cm)​B=Bm+1.\displaystyle A^{m}B=(B+C)^{m}B=(B^{m}+C^{m})B=B^{m+1}.

Similarly, we have Cm+1=Am​CC^{m+1}=A^{m}C. Therefore, if AN=0A^{N}=0 for some N≥1N\geq 1, we have BN+1=CN+1=0B^{N+1}=C^{N+1}=0.  □\Box

Note that, for the (⇐)(\Leftarrow) part of (b)(b) in Theorem 2.1, we need only a weaker condition. Namely, for any 1≤i,j≤n1\leq i,j\leq n,

⟨∇(Di​S),∇(Dj​T)⟩=⟨∇(Dj​S),∇(Di​T)⟩,\displaystyle\langle\nabla(D_{i}S),\nabla(D_{j}T)\rangle=\langle\nabla(D_{j}S),\nabla(D_{i}T)\rangle,

which will ensure that Hes ​(S)\text{Hes\,}(S) and Hes ​(T)\text{Hes\,}(T) commute.

To consider the second question 𝐐𝟐{\bf Q_{2}}, let us first fix the following notation.

For any P∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P\in\mathbb{C}[[z]], let 𝒜⁡(P){\mathcal{A}}(P) denote the subalgebra of ℂ⁡[[z]]\mathbb{C}[[z]] generated by all partial derivatives of PP (of any order). We also define a sequence {Q[m](z)|,m≥1}\{Q_{[m]}(z)\,|,m\geq 1\} by writing the deformed inversion pair Qt​(z)Q_{t}(z) of P⁡(z)P(z) as

(2.2) Qt​(z)=∑m≥1tm−1​Q[m]​(z).\displaystyle Q_{t}(z)=\sum_{m\geq 1}t^{m-1}Q_{[m]}(z).
Lemma 2.3.

For any P∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P\in\mathbb{C}[[z]], we have

(a)(a) 𝒜⁡(P){\mathcal{A}}(P) is closed under the action of any differential operator of ℂ⁡[z]\mathbb{C}[z] with constant coefficients.

(b)(b) For any m≥1m\geq 1, we have Q[m]​(z)∈𝒜​(P)Q_{[m]}(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}(P).

Proof:  (a)(a) Note that, by the definition of 𝒜⁡(P){\mathcal{A}}(P), a formal power series g⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]g(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[z]] lies in 𝒜⁡(P){\mathcal{A}}(P) iff it can be written (not necessarily uniquely) as a polynomial in partial derivatives of P⁡(z)P(z). Then, by the Leibniz Rule, it is easy to see that, for any g⁡(z)∈𝒜⁡(P)g(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}(P), Di​g​(z)∈𝒜⁡(P)D_{i}g(z)\in{\mathcal{A}}(P) (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n). Repeating this argument, we see that any partial derivative of g⁡(z)g(z) is in 𝒜⁡(P){\mathcal{A}}(P). Hence (a)(a) follows.

(b)(b) Recall that, by Proposition 3.73.7 in [Z1], we have the following recurrent formula for Q[m]​(z)Q_{[m]}(z) (m≥1)(m\geq 1) in general:

(2.3) Q[1]​(z)\displaystyle Q_{[1]}(z) =P⁡(z),\displaystyle=P(z),
(2.4) Q[m]​(z)\displaystyle Q_{[m]}(z) =12​(m−1)​∑k,l≥1k+l=m⟨∇Q[k]​(z),∇Q[l]​(z)⟩.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2(m-1)}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k,l\geq 1\\ k+l=m\end{subarray}}\langle\nabla Q_{[k]}(z),\nabla Q_{[l]}(z)\rangle.

for any m≥2m\geq 2.

By using (a)(a), the recurrent formulas above and induction on m≥1m\geq 1, it is easy to check that (b)(b) holds too.  □\Box

Definition 2.4.

For any S,T∈ℂ⁡[[z]]S,T\in\mathbb{C}[[z]], we say SS and TT are disjoint to each other if, for any g1∈𝒜⁡(S)g_{1}\in{\mathcal{A}}(S) and g2∈𝒜⁡(T)g_{2}\in{\mathcal{A}}(T), we have ⟨∇g1,∇g2⟩=0\langle\nabla g_{1},\nabla g_{2}\rangle=0.

This terminology will be justified in Section 8 when we consider a graph 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P) associated to homogeneous harmonic polynomials PP.

Lemma 2.5.

Let S,T∈ℂ⁡[[z]]S,T\in\mathbb{C}[[z]]. Then SS and TT are disjoint to each other iff, for any α,β∈ℕn\alpha,\beta\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}, we have

(2.5) ⟨∇(Dα​S),∇(Dβ​T)⟩=0.\displaystyle\langle\nabla(D^{\alpha}S),\nabla(D^{\beta}T)\rangle=0.

Proof:  The (⇒)(\Rightarrow) part of the lemma is trivial. Conversely, for any g1∈𝒜⁡(S)g_{1}\in{\mathcal{A}}(S) and g2∈𝒜⁡(T)g_{2}\in{\mathcal{A}}(T) (i=1,2)(i=1,2), we need show

⟨∇g1,∇g2⟩=0.\displaystyle\langle\nabla g_{1},\nabla g_{2}\rangle=0.

But this can be easily checked by, first, reducing to the case that g1g_{1} and g2g_{2} are monomials of partial derivatives of SS and TT, respectively, and then applying the Leibniz rule and Eq. (2.5)(\ref{p-inv-L3-e1}) above.  □\Box

A family of examples of disjoint polynomials or formal power series are given as in the following lemma, which will also be needed later in Section 8.

Lemma 2.6.

Let I1I_{1} and I2I_{2} be two finite subsets of ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} such that, for any αi∈Ii\alpha_{i}\in I_{i} (i=1,2)(i=1,2), we have ⟨α1,α2⟩=0\langle\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}\rangle=0. Denote by 𝒜i{\mathcal{A}}_{i} (i=1,2)(i=1,2) the completion of the subalgebra of ℂ⁡[[z]]\mathbb{C}[[z]] generated by hα​(z):=⟨α,z⟩h_{\alpha}(z)\!:=\langle\alpha,z\rangle (α∈Ii)(\alpha\in I_{i}), i.e. 𝒜i{\mathcal{A}}_{i} is the set of all formal power series in hα​(z)h_{\alpha}(z) (α∈Ii)(\alpha\in I_{i}) over ℂ\mathbb{C}. Then, for any Pi∈𝒜iP_{i}\in{\mathcal{A}}_{i} (i=1,2)(i=1,2), P1P_{1} and P2P_{2} are disjoint.

Proof:  First, by a similar argument as the proof for Lemma 2.3, (a)(a), it is easy to check that 𝒜i{\mathcal{A}}_{i} (i=1,2)(i=1,2) are closed under action of any differential operator with constant coefficients. Secondly, since 𝒜i{\mathcal{A}}_{i} (i=1,2)(i=1,2) are subalgebras of ℂ⁡[[z]]\mathbb{C}[[z]], we have 𝒜⁡(Pi)⊂𝒜i{\mathcal{A}}(P_{i})\subset{\mathcal{A}}_{i} (i=1,2)(i=1,2).

Now, for the second question 𝐐𝟐{\bf Q_{2}} on page Q 2 :, we have the following result.

=12​(m−1)​∑k,l≥1k+l=m⟨∇U[k]+∇V[k],∇U[l]+∇V[l]⟩\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2(m-1)}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k,l\geq 1\\ k+l=m\end{subarray}}\langle\nabla U_{[k]}+\nabla V_{[k]},\nabla U_{[l]}+\nabla V_{[l]}\rangle
Noting that, by Lemma 2.3, U[j]∈𝒜⁡(S)U_{[j]}\in{\mathcal{A}}(S) and V[j]∈𝒜⁡(T)V_{[j]}\in{\mathcal{A}}(T) (1≤j≤m)(1\leq j\leq m):
=12​(m−1)​∑k,l≥1k+l=m⟨∇U[k],∇U[l]⟩+12​(m−1)​∑k,l≥1k+l=m⟨∇V[k],∇V[l]⟩\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2(m-1)}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k,l\geq 1\\ k+l=m\end{subarray}}\langle\nabla U_{[k]},\nabla U_{[l]}\rangle+\frac{1}{2(m-1)}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k,l\geq 1\\ k+l=m\end{subarray}}\langle\nabla V_{[k]},\nabla V_{[l]}\rangle

=U[m]+V[m].\displaystyle=U_{[m]}+V_{[m]}.

Corollary 2.8.

Let Pi∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P_{i}\in\mathbb{C}[[z]] (1≤i≤k)(1\leq i\leq k) which are disjoint to each other. Set P=∑i=1kPiP=\sum_{i=1}^{k}P_{i}. Then, we have

3. Local Convergence of Deformed Inversion Pairs of Homogeneous (HN) Polynomials

Let P⁡(z)P(z) be a formal power series which is convergent near 0∈ℂn0\in\mathbb{C}^{n}. Then the associated symmetric map F⁡(z)=z−∇PF(z)=z-\nabla P is a well-defined analytic map from an open neighborhood of 0∈ℂn0\in\mathbb{C}^{n} to ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}. If we further assume that J​F​(0)=In×nJF(0)=I_{n\times n}, the formal inverse G​(z)=z+∇Q​(z)G(z)=z+\nabla Q(z) of F⁡(z)F(z) is also locally well-defined analytic map. So the inversion pair Q⁡(z)Q(z) of P⁡(z)P(z) is also locally convergent near 0∈ℂn0\in\mathbb{C}^{n}. In this section, we use the formulas Eqs. (2.4)(\ref{Recurr-2}), (1.1)(\ref{E-Q-1}) and the Cauchy estimates to derive some estimates for the radius of convergence of inversion pairs Q⁡(z)Q(z) of homogeneous (HN) polynomials P⁡(z)P(z) (see Propositions 3.1 and 3.3).

First let us fix the following notation.

For any a∈ℂna\in\mathbb{C}^{n} and r>0r>0, we denote by B⁡(a,r)B(a,r) (resp. S⁡(a,r)S(a,r)) the open ball (resp. the sphere) centered at a∈ℂa\in\mathbb{C} with radius r>0r>0. The unit sphere S⁡(0,1)S(0,1) will also be denoted by S2​n−1S^{2n-1}. Furthermore, we let Ω⁡(a,r)\Omega(a,r) be the polydisk centered at a∈ℂna\in\mathbb{C}^{n} with radius r>0r>0, i.e. Ω(a,r):={z∈ℂn||zi−ai|<r, 1≤i≤n}\Omega(a,r)\!:=\{z\in\mathbb{C}^{n}\,|\,|z_{i}-a_{i}|<r,\,1\leq i\leq n\}. For any subset A⊂ℂnA\subset\mathbb{C}^{n}, we will use A¯\bar{A} to denote the closure of AA in ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}.

For any polynomial P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z] and a compact subset D⊂ℂnD\subset\mathbb{C}^{n}, we set |P|D|P|_{D} to be the maximum value of |P⁡(z)||P(z)| over DD. In particular, when DD is the unit sphere S2​n−1S^{2n-1}, we also write |P|=|P|D|P|=|P|_{D}, i.e.

(3.1) |P|:=max⁡{|P⁡(z)||z∈S2​n−1}.\displaystyle|P|\!:=\max\{|P(z)|\,|\,z\in S^{2n-1}\}.

Note that, for any r≥0r\geq 0 and a∈B⁡(0,r)a\in B(0,r), we have Ω⁡(a,r)⊂B⁡(a,r)⊂B⁡(0,2​r)\Omega(a,r)\subset B(a,r)\subset B(0,2r). Combining with the well-known Maximum Principle of holomorphic functions, we get

4. Self-Inverting Formal Power Series

Note that, by the definition of inversion pairs (see page 1.1), Q∈ℂ⁡[[z]]Q\in\mathbb{C}[[z]] is the inversion pair of P∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P\in\mathbb{C}[[z]] iff PP is the inversion pair of QQ. In other words, the relation that QQ and PP are inversion pair of each other in some sense is a duality relation. Naturally, one may ask, for which P⁡(z)P(z), it is self-dual or self-inverting? In this section, we discuss this special family of polynomials or formal power series.

Another purpose of this section is to draw the reader’s attention to the problem of classification of (HN) self-inverting polynomials (see Open Problem 4.8). Even though the classification of HN polynomials seems to be out of reach at the current time, we believe that the classification of (HN) self-inverting polynomials is much more approachable.

Definition 4.1.

A formal power series P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[z]] with o⁡(P⁡(z))≥2o(P(z))\geq 2 and (Hes ​P)​(0)(\text{Hes\,}P)(0) nilpotent is said to be self-inverting if its inversion pair Q⁡(z)=P⁡(z)Q(z)=P(z).

Following the terminology introduced in [B], we say a formal map F⁡(z)=z−H⁡(z)F(z)=z-H(z) with H⁡(z)∈ℂ​[[z]]×nH(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[z]]^{\times n} and o⁡(H⁡(z))≥1o(H(z))\geq 1 is a quasi-translation if j​(F)​(0)≠0j(F)(0)\neq 0 and its formal inverse map is given by G⁡(z)=z+H⁡(z)G(z)=z+H(z).

Therefore, for any P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[z]] with o⁡(P⁡(z))≥2o(P(z))\geq 2 and (Hes ​P)​(0)(\text{Hes\,}P)(0) nilpotent, it is self-inverting iff the associated symmetric formal map F​(z)=z−∇P​(z)F(z)=z-\nabla P(z) is a quasi-translation.

For quasi-translations, the following general result has been proved in Proposition 1.11.1 of [B] for polynomial quasi-translations.

Proposition 4.2.

A formal map F⁡(z)=z−H⁡(z)F(z)=z-H(z) with o⁡(H)≥1o(H)\geq 1 and J​H​(0)JH(0) nilpotent is a quasi-translation if and only if J​H⋅H=0JH\cdot H=0.

Even though the proposition above was proved in [B] only in the setting of polynomial maps, the proof given there works equally well for formal quasi-translations under the condition that J​H​(0)JH(0) is nilpotent. Since it has also been shown in Proposition 1.11.1 in [B] that, for any polynomial quasi-translations F⁡(z)=z−H⁡(z)F(z)=z-H(z), J​H​(z)JH(z) is always nilpotent, so the condition that J​H​(0)JH(0) is nilpotent in the proposition above does not put any extra restriction for the case of polynomial quasi-translations.

From Proposition 4.2 above, we immediately have the following criterion for self-inverting formal power series.

Proposition 4.3.

For any P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[z]] with o⁡(P)≥2o(P)\geq 2 and (Hes ​P)​(0)(\text{Hes\,}P)(0) nilpotent, it is self-inverting if and only if ⟨∇P,∇P⟩=0\langle\nabla P,\nabla P\rangle=0.

Proof:  Since o⁡(P)≥2o(P)\geq 2 and (Hes ​P)​(0)(\text{Hes\,}P)(0) is nilpotent, by Proposition 4.2, we see that, P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[z]] is self-inverting iff J⁡(∇P)⋅∇P=(Hes ​P)⋅∇P=0J(\nabla P)\cdot\nabla P=(\text{Hes\,}P)\cdot\nabla P=0. But, on the other hand, it is easy to check that, for any P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[z]], we have the following identity:

(Hes P)⋅∇P=12∇⟨∇P,∇P⟩.\displaystyle(\text{Hes\,}P)\cdot\nabla P=\frac{1}{2}\nabla\langle\nabla P,\nabla P\rangle.

Therefore, (Hes ​P)⋅∇P=0(\text{Hes\,}P)\cdot\nabla P=0 iff ∇⟨∇P,∇P⟩=0\nabla\langle\nabla P,\nabla P\rangle=0, and iff ⟨∇P,∇P⟩=0\langle\nabla P,\nabla P\rangle=0 because o⁡(⟨∇P,∇P⟩)≥2o(\langle\nabla P,\nabla P\rangle)\geq 2.  □\Box

Corollary 4.4.

For any P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[z]] with o⁡(P)≥2o(P)\geq 2 and (Hes ​P)​(0)(\text{Hes\,}P)(0) nilpotent, if it is self-inverting, then so is Pm​(z)P^{m}(z) for any m≥1m\geq 1.

Proof:  Note that, for any m≥2m\geq 2, we have o⁡(Pm​(z))≥2​m>2o(P^{m}(z))\geq 2m>2 and (Hes ​P)​(0)=0(\text{Hes\,}P)(0)=0. Then, the corollary follows immediately from Proposition 4.3 and the following general identity:

(4.1) ⟨∇Pm,∇Pm⟩=m2​P2​m−2​⟨∇P,∇P⟩.\displaystyle\langle\nabla P^{m},\nabla P^{m}\rangle=m^{2}P^{2m-2}\langle\nabla P,\nabla P\rangle.

□\Box

Corollary 4.5.

For any harmonic formal power series P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[z]] with o⁡(P)≥2o(P)\geq 2 and (Hes ​P)​(0)(\text{Hes\,}P)(0) nilpotent, it is self-inverting iff Δ​P2=0\Delta P^{2}=0.

Proof:  This follows immediately from Proposition 4.3 and the following general identity:

(4.2) Δ​P2=2​(Δ​P)​P+2​⟨∇P,∇P⟩.\displaystyle\Delta P^{2}=2(\Delta P)P+2\langle\nabla P,\nabla P\rangle.

□\Box

Proposition 4.6.

Let P⁡(z)P(z) be a harmonic self-inverting formal power series. Then, for any m≥1m\geq 1, PmP^{m} is HN.

Proof:  First, we use the mathematical induction on m≥1m\geq 1 to show that Δ​Pm=0\Delta P^{m}=0 for any m≥1m\geq 1.

The case of m=1m=1 is given. For any m≥2m\geq 2, consider

Δ​Pm\displaystyle\Delta P^{m} =Δ⁡(P⋅Pm−1)\displaystyle=\Delta(P\cdot P^{m-1})
=(Δ​P)​Pm−1+P⁡(Δ​Pm−1)+2​⟨∇P,∇Pm−1⟩\displaystyle=(\Delta P)P^{m-1}+P(\Delta P^{m-1})+2\langle\nabla P,\nabla P^{m-1}\rangle
=(Δ​P)​Pm−1+P⁡(Δ​Pm−1)+2​(m−1)​Pm−2​⟨∇P,∇P⟩.\displaystyle=(\Delta P)P^{m-1}+P(\Delta P^{m-1})+2(m-1)P^{m-2}\langle\nabla P,\nabla P\rangle.

Then, by the mathematical induction assumption and Proposition 4.3, we get Δ​Pm=0\Delta P^{m}=0.

Secondly, for any fixed m≥1m\geq 1 and d≥1d\geq 1, we have

Δd​[(Pm)d]\displaystyle\Delta^{d}[(P^{m})^{d}] =Δd−1​(Δ​Pd​m)=0.\displaystyle=\Delta^{d-1}(\Delta P^{dm})=0.

Then, by the criterion in Proposition 1.2, PmP^{m} is HN.  □\Box

Example 4.7.

Note that, in Section 5.25.2 of [Z2], a family of self-inverting HN formal power series has been constructed as follows.

Let Ξ\Xi be any non-empty subset of ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} such that, for any α,β∈Ξ\alpha,\beta\in\Xi, ⟨α,β⟩=0\langle\alpha,\beta\rangle=0. Let 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} be the completion of the subalgebra of ℂ⁡[[z]]\mathbb{C}[[z]] generated by hα​(z):=⟨α,z⟩h_{\alpha}(z)\!:=\langle\alpha,z\rangle (α∈Ξ)(\alpha\in\Xi), i.e. 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} is the set of all formal power series in hα​(z)h_{\alpha}(z) (α∈Ξ)(\alpha\in\Xi) over ℂ\mathbb{C}. Then it is straightforward to check ((or see Section 5.25.2 of [Z2] for details)) that any element P⁡(z)∈𝒜P(z)\in{\mathcal{A}} is HN and self-inverting.

It is unknown if all HN self-inverting polynomials or formal power series can be obtained by the construction above. More generally, we believe the following open problem is worth investigating.

Open Problem 4.8.

(a)(a) Decide whether or not all self-inverting polynomials or formal power series are HN.

(b)(b) Classify all ((HN)) self-inverting polynomials and formal power series.

Finally, let us point out that, for any self-inverting P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[z]], the deformed inversion pair Qt​(z)Q_{t}(z) (not just Q​(z)=Qt=1​(z)Q(z)=Q_{t=1}(z)) is also same as P⁡(z)P(z).

Proposition 4.9.

Let P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[z]] with o⁡(P)≥2o(P)\geq 2 and (Hes ​P)​(0)(\text{Hes\,}P)(0) nilpotent. Then P⁡(z)P(z) is self-inverting if and only if Qt​(z)=P​(z)Q_{t}(z)=P(z).

Proof:  First, let us point out the following observations.

Let tt be a formal central parameter and Ft(z)=z−t∇P(z)F_{t}(z)=z-t\nabla P(z) as before. Since o⁡(P)≥2o(P)\geq 2 and (Hes ​P)​(0)(\text{Hes\,}P)(0) is nilpotent, we have j​(Ft)​(0)=1j(F_{t})(0)=1. Therefore, Ft​(z)F_{t}(z) is an automorphism of the algebra ℂ​[t]​[[z]]\mathbb{C}[t][[z]] of formal power series of zz over ℂ⁡[t]\mathbb{C}[t]. Since the inverse map of Ft​(z)F_{t}(z) is given by Gt(z)=z+t∇Qt(z)G_{t}(z)=z+t\nabla Q_{t}(z), we see that Qt​(z)∈ℂ⁡[t]​[[z]]Q_{t}(z)\in\mathbb{C}[t][[z]]. Therefore, for any t0∈ℂt_{0}\in\mathbb{C}, Qt=t0​(z)Q_{t=t_{0}}(z) makes sense and lies in ℂ⁡[[z]]\mathbb{C}[[z]]. Furthermore, by the uniqueness of inverse maps, it is easy to see that the inverse map of Ft0=z−t0∇PF_{t_{0}}=z-t_{0}\nabla P of ℂ​[t]​[[z]]\mathbb{C}[t][[z]] is given by Gt0(z)=z+t0∇Qt=t0G_{t_{0}}(z)=z+t_{0}\nabla Q_{t=t_{0}}. Therefore the inversion pair of t0​P​(z)t_{0}P(z) is given by t0​Qt=t0​(z)t_{0}Q_{t=t_{0}}(z).

With the notation and observations above, by choosing t0=1t_{0}=1, we have Qt=1​(z)=Q​(z)Q_{t=1}(z)=Q(z) and the (⇐)(\Leftarrow) part of the proposition follows immediately. Conversely, for any t0∈ℂt_{0}\in\mathbb{C}, we have ⟨∇(t0​P),∇(t0​P)⟩=t02​⟨∇P,∇P⟩\langle\nabla(t_{0}P),\nabla(t_{0}P)\rangle=t_{0}^{2}\langle\nabla P,\nabla P\rangle. Then, by Proposition 4.3, t0​P​(z)t_{0}P(z) is self-inverting and its inversion pair t0​Qt=t0​(z)t_{0}Q_{t=t_{0}}(z) is same as t0​P​(z)t_{0}P(z), i.e. t0​Qt=t0​(z)=t0​P​(z)t_{0}Q_{t=t_{0}}(z)=t_{0}P(z). Therefore, we have Qt=t0​(z)=P​(z)Q_{t=t_{0}}(z)=P(z) for any t0∈ℂ×t_{0}\in\mathbb{C}^{\times}. But on the other hand, we have Qt​(z)∈ℂ⁡[t]​[[z]]Q_{t}(z)\in\mathbb{C}[t][[z]] as pointed above, i.e. the coefficients of all monomials of zz in Qt​(z)Q_{t}(z) are polynomials of tt, hence we must have Qt​(z)=P​(z)Q_{t}(z)=P(z) which is the (⇒)(\Rightarrow) part of the proposition.  □\Box

5. The Vanishing Conjecture over Fields of Positive Characteristic

It is well-known that the JC may fail when F⁡(z)F(z) is not a polynomial map (e.g. F1​(z1,z2)=e−z1;F_{1}(z_{1},z_{2})=e^{-z_{1}}; F2​(z1,z2)=z2​ez1F_{2}(z_{1},z_{2})=z_{2}e^{z_{1}}). It also fails badly over fields of positive characteristic even in one variable case (e.g. F⁡(x)=x−xpF(x)=x-x^{p} over a field of characteristic p>0p>0). However, the situation for the VC over fields of positive characteristic is dramatically different from the JC even through these two conjectures are equivalent to each other over fields of characteristic zero. Actually, as we will show in the proposition below, the VC over fields of positive characteristic holds for any polynomials (not even necessarily HN) and also for any HN formal power series.

Proposition 5.1.

Let kk be a field of characteristic p>0p>0. Then

(a)(a) For any polynomial P⁡(z)∈k⁡[z]P(z)\in k[z] ((not necessarily homogeneous nor HN)) of degree d≥1d\geq 1,   Δm​Pm+1=0\Delta^{m}P^{m+1}=0 for any m≥d⁡(p−1)2m\geq\frac{d(p-1)}{2}.

(b)(b) For any HN formal power series P⁡(z)∈k⁡[[z]]P(z)\in k[[z]], i.e. Δm​Pm=0\Delta^{m}P^{m}=0 for any m≥1m\geq 1, we have, Δm​Pm+1=0\Delta^{m}P^{m+1}=0 for any m≥p−1m\geq p-1.

In other words, over the fields of positive characteristic, the VC holds even for HN formal power series P⁡(z)∈k⁡[[z]]P(z)\in k[[z]]; while for polynomials, it holds even without the HN condition nor any other conditions.

Proof:  The main reason that the proposition above holds is because of the following simple fact due to the Leibniz rule and positiveness of the characteristics of the base field kk, namely, for m≥1m\geq 1, u⁡(z),v⁡(z)∈k⁡[[z]]u(z),v(z)\in k[[z]] and any differential operator Λ\Lambda of k⁡[z]k[z], we have

(5.1) Λ⁡(um​p​v)=um​p​Λ​v.\displaystyle\Lambda(u^{mp}v)=u^{mp}\Lambda v.

Now let P⁡(z)P(z) be any polynomial or formal series as in the proposition. For any m≥1m\geq 1, write m+1=qm​p+rmm+1=q_{m}p+r_{m} with qm,rm∈ℤq_{m},r_{m}\in{\mathbb{Z}} and 0≤rm≤p−10\leq r_{m}\leq p-1. Then by Eq. (5.1)(\ref{pVC-MainThm-pe1}) , we have

(5.2) Δm​Pm+1=Δm​(Pqm​p​Prm)=Pqm​p​Δm​Prm.\displaystyle\Delta^{m}P^{m+1}=\Delta^{m}(P^{q_{m}p}P^{r_{m}})=P^{q_{m}p}\Delta^{m}P^{r_{m}}.

If P⁡(z)P(z) is a polynomial of degree d≥1d\geq 1, we have Δm​Prm=0\Delta^{m}P^{r_{m}}=0 when m≥d⁡(p−1)2m\geq\frac{d(p-1)}{2}, since in this case 2​m>deg⁡(Prm)2m>\deg(P^{r_{m}}). If P⁡(z)P(z) is a HN formal power series, we have Δm​Prm=0\Delta^{m}P^{r_{m}}=0 when m≥p−1≥rmm\geq p-1\geq r_{m}. Therefore, (a)(a) and (b)(b) in the proposition follow from Eq. (5.2)(\ref{pVC-MainThm-pe2}) and the observations above.  □\Box

One interesting question is whether or not the VC fails (as the JC does) for any HN formal power series P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[z]] but P⁡(z)∉ℂ⁡[z]P(z)\not\in\mathbb{C}[z]? To our best knowledge, no such counterexample has been known yet. We here put it as an open problem.

Open Problem 5.2.

Find a HN formal power series P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[z]] but P⁡(z)∉ℂ⁡[z]P(z)\not\in\mathbb{C}[z], if there are any, such that the VC fails for P⁡(z)P(z).

One final remark about Proposition 5.1 is as follows. Note that the crucial fact used in the proof is that any differential operator Λ\Lambda of k⁡[z]k[z] commutes with the multiplication operator by the pt​hp^{th} power of any element of k⁡[[z]]k[[z]]. Then, by a parallel argument as in the proof of Proposition 5.1, it is easy to see that the following more general result also holds.

Proposition 5.3.

Let kk be a field of characteristics p>0p>0 and Λ\Lambda a differential operator of k⁡[z]k[z]. Let f∈k⁡[[z]]f\in k[[z]]. Assume that, for any 1≤m≤p−11\leq m\leq p-1, there exists Nm>0N_{m}>0 such that ΛNm​fm=0\Lambda^{N_{m}}f^{m}=0. Then, we have Λm​fm+1=0\Lambda^{m}f^{m+1}=0 when m>>0m>>0.

In particular, if Λ\Lambda strictly decreases the degree of polynomials. Then, for any polynomial f∈k⁡[z]f\in k[z], we have Λm​fm+1=0\Lambda^{m}f^{m+1}=0 when m>>0m>>0.

6. A Criterion of Hessian Nilpotency for Homogeneous Polynomials

Recall that ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle denotes the standard ℂ\mathbb{C} bilinear form of ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}. For any β∈ℂn\beta\in\mathbb{C}^{n}, we set hβ​(z):=⟨β,z⟩h_{\beta}(z)\!:=\langle\beta,z\rangle and βD:=⟨β,D⟩\beta_{D}\!:=\langle\beta,D\rangle.

The main result of this section is the following criterion of Hessian nilpotency for homogeneous polynomials. Considering the criterion given in Proposition 1.2, it is somewhat surprising but the proof turns out to be very simple.

Theorem 6.1.

For any β∈ℂn\beta\in\mathbb{C}^{n} and homogeneous polynomial P⁡(z)P(z) of degree d≥2d\geq 2, set Pβ​(z):=βDd−2​P​(z)P_{\beta}(z)\!:=\beta_{D}^{d-2}P(z). Then, we have

(6.1) Hes ​Pβ=(d−2)!​(Hes ​P)​(β).\displaystyle{\text{Hes\,}P_{\beta}}=(d-2)!\,(\text{Hes\,}P)(\beta).

In particular, P⁡(z)P(z) is HN iff, for any β∈ℂn\beta\in\mathbb{C}^{n}, Pβ​(z)P_{\beta}(z) is HN.

To prove the theorem, we need first the following lemma.

Lemma 6.2.

Let β∈ℂn\beta\in\mathbb{C}^{n} and P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z] homogeneous of degree N≥1N\geq 1. Then

(6.2) βDN​P​(z)=N!​P​(β).\displaystyle\beta_{D}^{N}P(z)=N!\,P(\beta).

Proof:  Since both sides of Eq. (6.2)(\ref{crn-L1-e1}) are linear on P⁡(z)P(z), we may assume P⁡(z)P(z) is a monomial, say P⁡(z)=z𝐚P(z)=z^{\bf a} for some 𝐚∈ℕn{\bf a}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n} with |𝐚|=N|{\bf a}|=N.

Consider

βDN​P​(z)\displaystyle\beta_{D}^{N}P(z) =(∑i=1nβi​Di)N​z𝐚=∑𝐤∈ℕn|𝐤|=NnN!𝐤!​β𝐤​D𝐤​z𝐚\displaystyle=(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\beta_{i}D_{i})^{N}z^{\bf a}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\bf k}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}\\ |{\bf k}|=N\end{subarray}}^{n}\frac{N!}{{\bf k}!}\beta^{\bf k}D^{\bf k}z^{\bf a}
=N!𝐚!​β𝐚​D𝐚​z𝐚=N!​β𝐚=N!​P​(β).\displaystyle=\frac{N!}{{\bf a}!}\beta^{\bf a}D^{\bf a}z^{\bf a}=N!\beta^{\bf a}=N!P(\beta).

□\Box

Proof of Theorem 6.1: We consider

Hes ​Pβ​(z)\displaystyle\text{Hes\,}P_{\beta}(z) =(∂2(βDd−2​P)∂zi​∂zj​(z))n×n=(βDd−2​∂2P∂zi​∂zj​(z))n×n\displaystyle=\left(\frac{\partial^{2}(\beta_{D}^{d-2}P)}{\partial z_{i}\partial z_{j}}(z)\right)_{n\times n}=\left(\beta_{D}^{d-2}\frac{\partial^{2}P}{\partial z_{i}\partial z_{j}}(z)\right)_{n\times n}
Applying Lemma 6.2 to ∂2P∂zi​∂zj​(z)\frac{\partial^{2}P}{\partial z_{i}\partial z_{j}}(z):
=(d−2)!​(∂2P∂zi​∂zj​(β))n×n=(d−2)!​(Hes ​P)​(β).\displaystyle=(d-2)!\left(\frac{\partial^{2}P}{\partial z_{i}\partial z_{j}}(\beta)\right)_{n\times n}=(d-2)!\,(\text{Hes\,}P)(\beta).

□\Box

Let {ei| 1≤i≤n}\{e_{i}\,|\,1\leq i\leq n\} be the standard basis of ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}. Applying the theorem above to β=ei\beta=e_{i} (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n), we have the following corollary, which was first proved by M. Kumar [K].

Corollary 6.3.

For any homogeneous HN polynomial P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z] of degree d≥2d\geq 2, Did−2​P​(z)D_{i}^{d-2}P(z) (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n) are also HN.

The reason that we think the criteria given in Theorem 6.1 and Corollary 6.3 interesting is that, Pβ​(z)=βDd−2​P​(z)P_{\beta}(z)=\beta_{D}^{d-2}P(z) is homogeneous of degree 22, and it is much easier to decide whether a homogeneous polynomial of degree 22 is HN or not. More precisely, for any homogeneous polynomial U⁡(z)U(z) of degree 22, there exists a unique symmetric n×nn\times n matrix AA such that U⁡(z)=zτ​A​zU(z)=z^{\tau}Az. Then it is easy to check that Hes ​U​(z)=2​A.\text{Hes\,}U(z)=2A. Therefore, U⁡(z)U(z) is HN iff the symmetric matrix AA is nilpotent.

Finally we end this section with the following open question on the criterion given in Proposition 1.2.

Recall that Proposition 1.2 was proved in [Z2]. We now sketch the argument.

For any m≥1m\geq 1, we set

(6.3) um​(P)\displaystyle u_{m}(P) =Tr Hesm​(P),\displaystyle=\text{Tr\,}\text{Hes}^{m}(P),
(6.4) vm​(P)\displaystyle v_{m}(P) =Δm​Pm.\displaystyle=\Delta^{m}P^{m}.

For any k≥1k\geq 1, we define 𝒰k​(P){\mathcal{U}}_{k}(P) (resp. 𝒱k​(P){\mathcal{V}}_{k}(P)) to be the ideal in ℂ⁡[[z]]\mathbb{C}[[z]] generated by {um​(P)|1≤m≤k}\{u_{m}(P)|1\leq m\leq k\} (resp. {vm​(P)|1≤m≤k}\{v_{m}(P)|1\leq m\leq k\}) and all their partial derivatives of any order. Then it has been shown (in a more general setting) in Section 44 in [Z2] that 𝒰k​(P)=𝒱k​(P)\mathcal{U}_{k}(P)=\mathcal{V}_{k}(P) for any k≥1k\geq 1.

It is well-known in linear algebra that, if um​(P​(z))=0u_{m}(P(z))=0 when m>>0m>>0, then Hes ​P\text{Hes\,}P is nilpotent and um​(P)=0u_{m}(P)=0 for any m≥1m\geq 1. One natural question is whether or not this is also the case for the sequence {vm​(P)|m≥1}\{v_{m}(P)\,|\,m\geq 1\}. More precisely, we believe the following conjecture which was proposed in [Z2] is worth investigating.

Conjecture 6.4.

Let P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[z]] with o⁡(P⁡(z))≥2o(P(z))\geq 2. If Δm​Pm​(z)=0\Delta^{m}P^{m}(z)=0 for m>>0m>>0, then P⁡(z)P(z) is HN.

7. Some Results on Symmetric Polynomial Maps

Let P⁡(z)P(z) be any formal power series with o⁡(P⁡(z))≥2o(P(z))\geq 2 and (Hes ​P)​(0)(\text{Hes\,}P)(0) nilpotent, and F⁡(z)F(z) and G⁡(z)G(z) as before. Set

(7.1) σ2:\displaystyle\sigma_{2}\!: =∑i=1nzi2,\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}^{2},
(7.2) f⁡(z):\displaystyle f(z)\!: =12​σ2−P⁡(z).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sigma_{2}-P(z).

Professors Mohan Kumar [K] and David Wright [Wr3] once asked how to write P⁡(z)P(z) and f⁡(z)f(z) in terms of F⁡(z)F(z)? More precisely, find U⁡(z),V⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]U(z),V(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[z]] such that

(7.3) U⁡(F⁡(z))\displaystyle U(F(z)) =P⁡(z),\displaystyle=P(z),
(7.4) V⁡(F⁡(z))\displaystyle V(F(z)) =f⁡(z).\displaystyle=f(z).

In this section, we first derive in Proposition 7.2 some explicit formulas for U⁡(z)U(z) and V⁡(z)V(z), and also for W⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[[z]]W(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[z]] such that

(7.5) W⁡(F⁡(z))=σ2​(z).\displaystyle W(F(z))=\sigma_{2}(z).

We then show in Theorem 7.4 that, when P⁡(z)P(z) is a HN polynomial, the VC holds for PP or equivalently, the JC holds for the associated symmetric polynomial map F⁡(z)=z−∇PF(z)=z-\nabla P, iff one of UU, VV and WW is polynomial.

8. A Graph Associated with Homogeneous HN Polynomials

In this section, we would like to draw the reader’s attention to a graph 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P) assigned to each homogeneous harmonic polynomials P⁡(z)P(z). The graph 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P) was first proposed by the author and later was further studied by R. Willems in his master thesis [Wi] under direction of Professor A. van den Essen. The introduction of the graph 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P) is mainly motivated by a criterion of Hessian nilpotency given in [Z2] (see also Theorem 8.2 below), via which one hopes more necessary or sufficient conditions for a homogeneous harmonic polynomial P⁡(z)P(z) to be HN can be obtained or described in terms of the graph structure of 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P).

We first give in Subsection 8.1 the definition of the graph 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P) for any homogeneous harmonic polynomial P⁡(z)P(z) and discuss the connectedness reduction (see Corollary 8.5), i.e. a reduction of the VC to the homogeneous HN polynomials PP such that 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P) is connected. We then consider in Subsection 8.2 a connection of 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P) with the tree expansion formula derived in [M] and [Wr2] for the inversion pair Q⁡(z)Q(z) of P⁡(z)P(z) (see Proposition 8.9). As an application of the connection, we give another proof for the connectedness reduction given in Corollary 8.5.

8.1. Definition and the Connectedness Reduction

For any β∈ℂn\beta\in\mathbb{C}^{n}, set hβ​(z):=⟨β,z⟩h_{\beta}(z)\!:=\langle\beta,z\rangle and βD:=⟨β,D⟩\beta_{D}\!:=\langle\beta,D\rangle, where ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle is the standard ℂ\mathbb{C}-bilinear form of ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}. Let X⁡(ℂ)X(\mathbb{C}) denote the set of all isotropic elements of ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}, i.e. the set of all elements α∈ℂn\alpha\in\mathbb{C}^{n} such that ⟨α,α⟩=0\langle\alpha,\alpha\rangle=0.

Recall that we have the following fundamental theorem on homogeneous harmonic polynomials.

Theorem 8.1.

For any homogeneous harmonic polynomial P⁡(z)P(z) of degree d≥2d\geq 2, we have

(8.1) P⁡(z)=∑i=1kci​hαid​(z)\displaystyle P(z)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}c_{i}h_{\alpha_{i}}^{d}(z)

for some ci∈ℂ×c_{i}\in\mathbb{C}^{\times} and αi∈X⁡(ℂn)\alpha_{i}\in X(\mathbb{C}^{n}) (1≤i≤k)(1\leq i\leq k).

Note that, replacing αi\alpha_{i} in Eq. (8.1) by ci−1d​αic_{i}^{-\frac{1}{d}}\alpha_{i}, we may also write P⁡(z)P(z) as

(8.2) P⁡(z)=∑i=1khαid​(z)\displaystyle P(z)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}h_{\alpha_{i}}^{d}(z)

with αi∈X⁡(ℂn)\alpha_{i}\in X(\mathbb{C}^{n}) (1≤i≤k)(1\leq i\leq k).

For the proof of Theorem 8.1, see, for example, [I] and [Wi].

We fix a homogeneous harmonic polynomial P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z] of degree d≥2d\geq 2, and assume that P⁡(z)P(z) is given by Eq. (8.2) for some αi∈X⁡(ℂn)\alpha_{i}\in X(\mathbb{C}^{n}) (1≤i≤k)(1\leq i\leq k). We may and will always assume {hαid​(z)|1≤i≤k}\{h_{\alpha_{i}}^{d}(z)|1\leq i\leq k\} are linearly independent in ℂ⁡[z]\mathbb{C}[z].

Recall the following matrices had been introduced in [Z2]:

(8.3) AP\displaystyle A_{P} =(⟨αi,αj⟩)k×k,\displaystyle=(\langle\alpha_{i},\alpha_{j}\rangle)_{k\times k},
(8.4) ΨP\displaystyle\Psi_{P} =(⟨αi,αj⟩​hαjd−2​(z))k×k.\displaystyle=(\langle\alpha_{i},\alpha_{j}\rangle h_{\alpha_{j}}^{d-2}(z))_{k\times k}.

Then we have the following criterion of Hessian nilpotency for homogeneous harmonic polynomials. For its proof, see Theorem 4.34.3 in [Z2].

Theorem 8.2.

Let P⁡(z)P(z) be as above. Then, for any m≥1m\geq 1, we have

(8.5) Tr Hes m​(P)=(d⁡(d−1))m​Tr ​ΨPm.\displaystyle\text{Tr\,}\text{Hes\,}^{m}(P)=(d(d-1))^{m}\text{Tr\,}\Psi_{P}^{m}.

In particular, P⁡(z)P(z) is HN if and only if the matrix ΨP\Psi_{P} is nilpotent.

One simple remark on the criterion above is as follows.

Let BB be the k×kk\times k diagonal matrix with the it​hi^{th} (1≤i≤k)(1\leq i\leq k) diagonal entry being hαi​(z)h_{\alpha_{i}}(z). For any 1≤j≤k1\leq j\leq k, set

(8.6) ΨP;j:=Bj​AP​Bd−2−j=(hαij​⟨αi,αj⟩​hαjd−2−j).\displaystyle\Psi_{P;j}\!:=B^{j}A_{P}B^{d-2-j}=(h_{\alpha_{i}}^{j}\langle\alpha_{i},\alpha_{j}\rangle h_{\alpha_{j}}^{d-2-j}).

Then, by repeatedly applying the fact that, for any two k×kk\times k matrices CC and DD, C​DCD is nilpotent iff so is D​CDC, it is easy to see that Theorem 8.2 can also be re-stated as follows.

Corollary 8.3.

Let P⁡(z)P(z) be given by Eq. (8.2)(\ref{d-Form}) with d≥2d\geq 2. Then, for any 1≤j≤d−21\leq j\leq d-2 and m≥1m\geq 1, we have

(8.7) Tr Hes m​(P)=(d⁡(d−1))m​Tr ​ΨP;jm.\displaystyle\text{Tr\,}\text{Hes\,}^{m}(P)=(d(d-1))^{m}\text{Tr\,}\Psi_{P;j}^{m}.

In particular, P⁡(z)P(z) is HN if and only if the matrix ΨP;j\Psi_{P;j} is nilpotent.

Note that, when dd is even, we may choose j=(d−2)/2j=(d-2)/2. So PP is HN iff the symmetric matrix

(8.8) ΨP;(d−2)/2​(z)=(hαi(d−2)/2​(z)​⟨αi,αj⟩​hαj(d−2)/2​(z))\displaystyle\Psi_{P;(d-2)/2}(z)=(\,h_{\alpha_{i}}^{(d-2)/2}(z)\,\langle\alpha_{i},\alpha_{j}\rangle\,h_{\alpha_{j}}^{(d-2)/2}(z)\,)

is nilpotent.

Motivated by the criterion above, we assign a graph 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P) to any homogeneous harmonic polynomial P⁡(z)P(z) as follows.

We fix an expression as in Eq. (8.2)(\ref{d-Form}) for P⁡(z)P(z). The set of vertices of 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P) will be the set of positive integers [𝐤]:={1,2,…,k}[{\bf k}]\!:=\{1,2,\dots,k\}. The vertices i and j of 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P) are connected by an edge iff ⟨αi,αj⟩≠0\langle\alpha_{i},\alpha_{j}\rangle\neq 0. In this case, we get a finite graph.

Furthermore, we may also label edges of 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P) by assigning ⟨αi,αj⟩\langle\alpha_{i},\alpha_{j}\rangle or (hαi(d−2)/2​⟨αi,αj⟩​hαi(d−2)/2)(h_{\alpha_{i}}^{(d-2)/2}\langle\alpha_{i},\alpha_{j}\rangle h_{\alpha_{i}}^{(d-2)/2}), when dd is even, for the edge connecting vertices i,j∈[𝐤]i,j\in[\bf k]. We then get a labeled graph whose adjacency matrix is exactly APA_{P} or ΨP,(d−2)/2\Psi_{P,(d-2)/2} (depending on the labels we choose for the edges of 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P)).

Naturally, one may also ask the following (open) questions.

Open Problem 8.4.

(a)(a) Find some necessary or sufficient conditions on the ((labeled)) graph 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P) such that the homogeneous harmonic polynomial P⁡(z)P(z) is HN.

(b)(b) Find some necessary or sufficient conditions on the (l​a​b​e​l​e​d)(labeled) graph 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P) such that the VC holds for the homogeneous HN polynomial P⁡(z)P(z).

First, let us point out that, to approach the open problems above, it will be enough to focus on homogeneous harmonic polynomials PP such that the graph 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P) is connected.

Suppose that the graph 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P) is a disconnected graph with r≥2r\geq 2 connected components. Let [𝐤]=⊔i=1rIi[{\bf k}]=\sqcup_{i=1}^{r}I_{i} be the corresponding partition of the set [𝐤][\bf k] of vertices of 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P). For each 1≤i≤r1\leq i\leq r, we set Pi​(z):=∑α∈Iihαd​(z)P_{i}(z)\!:=\sum_{\alpha\in I_{i}}h_{\alpha}^{d}(z).

Note that, by Lemma 2.6, PiP_{i} (1≤i≤r)(1\leq i\leq r) are disjoint to each other, so Corollary 2.8 applies to the sum P=∑i=1rPiP=\sum_{i=1}^{r}P_{i}. In particular, we have,

(a)(a) PP is HN iff each PiP_{i} is HN.

(b)(b) if the VC holds for each PiP_{i}, then it also holds for PP.

Therefore, we have the following connectedness reduction.

Corollary 8.5.

To study homogeneous HN polynomials PP or the VC for homogeneous HN polynomials PP, it will be enough to consider the case when 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P) is connected.

Note that, the property (a)(a) above was first proved by R. Willems ([Wi]) by using the criterion in Theorem 8.2. (b)(b) was first proved by the author by a different argument, and with the author’s permission, it had also been included in [Wi].

Finally, let us point out that R. Willems ([Wi]) has proved the following very interesting results on Open Problem 8.4.

Theorem 8.6.

(([Wi])) Let PP be a homogeneous HN polynomial as in Eq.(8.2)(\ref{d-Form}) with d≥4d\geq 4. Let l⁡(P)l(P) be the dimension of the vector subspace of ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} spanned by {αi| 1≤i≤k}\{\alpha_{i}\,|\,1\leq i\leq k\}. Then

  1. (1)

    If l⁡(P)=1,2,k−1l(P)=1,2,k-1 or kk, the graph 𝔾⁡(P){\mathbb{G}}(P) is totally disconnected ((i.e. 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P) is the graph with no edges)).

  2. (2)

    If l⁡(P)=k−2l(P)=k-2 and 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P) is connected, then 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P) is the complete bi-graph K⁡(4,k−4)K(4,k-4).

  3. (3)

    In the case of (a)(a) and (b)(b) above, the VC holds.

Furthermore, it has also been shown in [Wi] that, for any homogeneous HN polynomials PP, the graph 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P) can not be any path nor cycles of any positive length. For more details, see [Wi].

8.2. Connection with the Tree Expansion Formula of Inversion Pairs

First let us recall the tree expansion formula derived in [M], [Wr2] for the inversion pair Q⁡(z)Q(z).

Let 𝕋{\mathbb{T}} denote the set of all trees, i.e. the set of all connected and simply connected finite simple graphs. For each tree T∈𝕋T\in{\mathbb{T}}, denote by V⁡(T)V(T) and E⁡(T)E(T) the sets of all vertices and edges of TT, respectively. Then we have the following tree expansion formula for inversion pairs.

Theorem 8.7.

(([M], [Wr2])) Let P∈ℂ⁡[[z]]P\in\mathbb{C}[[z]] with o⁡(P)≥2o(P)\geq 2 and QQ its inversion pair. For any T∈𝕋T\in{\mathbb{T}}, set

(8.9) QT,P=∑ℓ:E⁡(T)→[𝐧]∏v∈V⁡(T)Da​d​j​(v),ℓP,\displaystyle Q_{T,P}=\sum_{\ell:E(T)\to[\bf n]}\prod_{v\in V(T)}D_{adj(v),\ell}P,

where a​d​j​(v)adj(v) is the set {e1,e2,…,es}\{e_{1},e_{2},\dots,e_{s}\} of edges of TT adjacent to vv, and Da​d​j​(v),ℓ=Dℓ⁡(e1)Dℓ⁡(e2)⋯Dℓ⁡(es)D_{adj(v),\ell}=D_{\ell(e_{1})}D_{\ell(e_{2})}\cdots D_{\ell(e_{s})}.

Then the inversion pair QQ of PP is given by

(8.10) Q=∑T∈𝕋1|A​u​t​(T)|​QT,P.\displaystyle Q=\sum_{T\in{\mathbb{T}}}\frac{1}{|Aut(T)|}Q_{T,P}.

Now we assume P⁡(z)P(z) is a homogeneous harmonic polynomial d≥2d\geq 2 and has expression in Eq. (8.2)(\ref{d-Form}). Under this assumption, it is easy to see that QT,PQ_{T,P} (T∈𝕋)(T\in{\mathbb{T}}) becomes

(8.11) QT,P=∑f:V⁡(T)→[𝐤]∑ℓ:E⁡(T)→[𝐧]∏v∈V⁡(T)Da​d​j​(v),ℓhαf⁡(v)d(z).\displaystyle Q_{T,P}=\sum_{f:V(T)\to[\bf k]}\sum_{\ell:E(T)\to[\bf n]}\prod_{v\in V(T)}D_{adj(v),\ell}h_{\alpha_{f(v)}}^{d}(z).

The role played by the graph 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P) of PP is to restrict the maps f:V⁡(T)→V⁡(𝒢⁡(P))(=[𝐤])f:V(T)\to V({\mathcal{G}}(P))(=[\bf k]) in Eq. (8.11)(\ref{QTP-1}) to a special family of maps. To be more precise, let Ω⁡(T,𝒢⁡(P))\Omega(T,{\mathcal{G}}(P)) be the set of maps f:V⁡(T)→[𝐤]f:V(T)\to[\bf k] such that, for any distinct adjoint vertices u,v∈V⁡(T)u,v\in V(T), f⁡(u)f(u) and f⁡(v)f(v) are distinct and adjoint in 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P). Then we have the following lemma.

Lemma 8.8.

For any f:V⁡(T)→[𝐤]f:V(T)\to[\bf k] with f∉Ω⁡(T,𝒢⁡(P))f\not\in\Omega(T,{\mathcal{G}}(P)), we have

(8.12) ∑ℓ:E⁡(T)→[𝐧]∏v∈V⁡(T)Da​d​j​(v),ℓhαf⁡(v)d(z)=0.\displaystyle\sum_{\ell:E(T)\to[\bf n]}\prod_{v\in V(T)}D_{adj(v),\ell}h_{\alpha_{f(v)}}^{d}(z)=0.

Proof:  Let f:V⁡(T)→[𝐤]f:V(T)\to[\bf k] as in the lemma. Since f∉Ω⁡(T,𝒢⁡(P))f\not\in\Omega(T,{\mathcal{G}}(P)), there exist distinct adjoint v1,v2∈V⁡(T)v_{1},v_{2}\in V(T) such that, either f⁡(v1)=f⁡(v2)f(v_{1})=f(v_{2}) or f⁡(v1)f(v_{1}) and f⁡(v2)f(v_{2}) are not adjoint in the graph 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P). In any case, we have ⟨αf⁡(v1),αf⁡(v2)⟩=0\langle\alpha_{f(v_{1})},\alpha_{f(v_{2})}\rangle=0.

Next we consider contributions to the RHS of Eq. (8.11)(\ref{QTP-1}) from the vertices v1v_{1} and v2v_{2}. Denote by ee the edge of TT connecting v1v_{1} and v2v_{2}, and {e1,…​er}\{e_{1},\dots e_{r}\} (resp. {e~1,…​e~s}\{\tilde{e}_{1},\dots\tilde{e}_{s}\}) the set of edges connected with v1v_{1} (resp. v2v_{2}) besides the edge ee. Then, for any ℓ:E⁡(T)→[𝐧]\ell:E(T)\to[\bf n], the factor in the RHS of Eq. (8.11)(\ref{QTP-1}) from the vertices v1v_{1} and v2v_{2} is the product

(8.13) (Dℓ⁡(e)Dℓ⁡(e1)⋯Dℓ⁡(er)hαf⁡(v1)d(z))(Dℓ⁡(e)Dℓ⁡(e~1)⋯Dℓ⁡(e~s)hαf⁡(v2)d(z)).\displaystyle\left(D_{\ell(e)}D_{\ell(e_{1})}\cdots D_{\ell(e_{r})}h_{\alpha_{f(v_{1})}}^{d}(z)\right)\left(D_{\ell(e)}D_{\ell(\tilde{e}_{1})}\cdots D_{\ell(\tilde{e}_{s})}h_{\alpha_{f(v_{2})}}^{d}(z)\right).

Define an equivalent relation for maps ℓ:E⁡(T)→[𝐧]\ell:E(T)\to[\bf n] by setting ℓ1∼ℓ2\ell_{1}\sim\ell_{2} iff ℓ1\ell_{1}, ℓ2\ell_{2} have same image at each edge of TT except ee. Then, by taking sum of the terms in Eq. (8.13)(\ref{PFEQ-1}) over each equivalent class, we get the factor

(8.14) ⟨∇Dℓ⁡(e1)⋯Dℓ⁡(er)hαf⁡(v1)d(z),∇Dℓ⁡(e~1)⋯Dℓ⁡(e~s)hαf⁡(v2)d(z)⟩.\displaystyle\left\langle\nabla D_{\ell(e_{1})}\cdots D_{\ell(e_{r})}h_{\alpha_{f(v_{1})}}^{d}(z),\,\nabla D_{\ell(\tilde{e}_{1})}\cdots D_{\ell(\tilde{e}_{s})}h_{\alpha_{f(v_{2})}}^{d}(z)\right\rangle.

Note that Dℓ⁡(e1)⋯Dℓ⁡(er)hαf⁡(v1)d(z)D_{\ell(e_{1})}\cdots D_{\ell(e_{r})}h_{\alpha_{f(v_{1})}}^{d}(z) and Dℓ⁡(e~1)⋯Dℓ⁡(e~s)hαf⁡(v2)d(z)D_{\ell(\tilde{e}_{1})}\cdots D_{\ell(\tilde{e}_{s})}h_{\alpha_{f(v_{2})}}^{d}(z) are constant multiples of some integral powers of hαf⁡(v1)​(z)h_{\alpha_{f(v_{1})}}(z) and hαf⁡(v2)​(z)h_{\alpha_{f(v_{2})}}(z), respectively. Therefore, ⟨αf⁡(v1),αf⁡(v2)⟩(=0)\langle\alpha_{f(v_{1})},\alpha_{f(v_{2})}\rangle(=0) appears as a multiplicative constant factor in the term in Eq. (8.14)(\ref{PFEQ-2}), which makes the term zero. Hence the lemma follows.  □\Box

One immediate consequence of the lemma above is the following proposition.

Proposition 8.9.

With the setting and notation as above, we have

(8.15) QT,P=∑f∈Ω⁡(T,𝒢⁡(P))∑ℓ:E⁡(T)→[𝐧]∏v∈V⁡(T)Da​d​j​(v),ℓhαf⁡(v)d(z).\displaystyle Q_{T,P}=\sum_{f\in\Omega(T,{\mathcal{G}}(P))}\,\sum_{\ell:E(T)\to[\bf n]}\prod_{v\in V(T)}D_{adj(v),\ell}h_{\alpha_{f(v)}}^{d}(z).
Remark 8.10.

(a)(a) For any f∈Ω⁡(T,𝒢⁡(P))f\in\Omega(T,{\mathcal{G}}(P)), {f−1​(j)|j∈Im​(f)}\{f^{-1}(j)\,|\,j\in\mbox{Im}(f)\} gives a partition of V⁡(T)V(T) since no two distinct vertices in f−1​(j)f^{-1}(j) (j∈Im​(f))(j\in\mbox{Im}(f)) can be adjoint. In other words, ff is nothing but a proper coloring for the tree TT, which is also subject to certain more conditions from the graph structure of 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P). It is interesting to see that the coloring problem of graphs also plays a role in the inversion problem of symmetric formal maps.

(b)(b) It will be interesting to see if more results can be derived from the graph 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P) via the formulas in Eqs. (8.10)(\ref{Me-Wr-eq1}) and (8.15)(\ref{QTP-2}).

Remark 8.11.

By similar arguments as those in proofs of Lemma 8.8, one may get another proof for Theorem 2.7 in the setting as in Lemma 2.6.

Finally, as an application of Proposition 8.9 above, we give another proof for the connectedness reduction given in Corollary 8.5.

Let PP as given in Eq. (8.2)(\ref{d-Form}) with the inversion pair QQ. Suppose that there exists a partition [𝐤]=I1⊔I2[{\bf k}]=I_{1}\sqcup I_{2} with Ii≠∅I_{i}\neq\emptyset. Let Pi=∑α∈Iihαd​(z)P_{i}=\sum_{\alpha\in I_{i}}h_{\alpha}^{d}(z) (i=1,2)(i=1,2) and QiQ_{i} the inversion pair of PiP_{i}. Then we have P=P1+P2P=P_{1}+P_{2} and 𝒢⁡(P1)⊔𝒢⁡(P2)=𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P_{1})\sqcup{\mathcal{G}}(P_{2})={\mathcal{G}}(P). Therefore, to show the connectedness reduction discussed in the previous subsection, it will be enough to show Q=Q1+Q2Q=Q_{1}+Q_{2}. But this will follow immediately from Eqs. (8.10)(\ref{Me-Wr-eq1}), (8.15)(\ref{QTP-2}) and the following lemma.

Lemma 8.12.

Let PP, P1P_{1} and P2P_{2} as above, then, for any tree T∈𝕋T\in{\mathbb{T}}, we have

Ω⁡(T,𝒢⁡(P))=Ω⁡(T,𝒢⁡(P1))⊔Ω⁡(T,𝒢⁡(P2)).\displaystyle\Omega(T,{\mathcal{G}}(P))=\Omega(T,{\mathcal{G}}(P_{1}))\sqcup\Omega(T,{\mathcal{G}}(P_{2})).

Proof:  For any f∈Ω⁡(T,𝒢⁡(P))f\in\Omega(T,{\mathcal{G}}(P)), ff preserves the adjacency of vertices of 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P). Since TT as a graph is connected, Im​(f)⊂V​(𝒢​(P))\mbox{Im}(f)\subset V({\mathcal{G}}(P)) as a (full) subgraph of 𝒢⁡(P){\mathcal{G}}(P) must also be connected. Therefore, Im​(f)⊂V⁡(𝒢⁡(P1))\mbox{Im}(f)\subset V({\mathcal{G}}(P_{1})) or Im​(f)⊂V⁡(𝒢⁡(P2))\mbox{Im}(f)\subset V({\mathcal{G}}(P_{2})). Hence Ω⁡(T,𝒢⁡(P))⊂Ω⁡(T,𝒢⁡(P1))⊔Ω⁡(T,𝒢⁡(P2))\Omega(T,{\mathcal{G}}(P))\subset\Omega(T,{\mathcal{G}}(P_{1}))\sqcup\Omega(T,{\mathcal{G}}(P_{2})). The other way of containess is obvious.  □\Box
